podcast.title: Lawsuit for Royalties
podcast.body: Andrew Loog Oldham, who was the original manager of The Rolling Stones, sued The Verve, claiming they owed him $1.7 million in royalties for "Bittersweet Symphony" due to the use of a five-note progression from his orchestra's version of "The Last Time." "Lugoldem figured he was owed $1.7 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Orchestral Interpretations for Easy Listening
podcast.body: The Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra created orchestral versions of The Rolling Stones' songs, released in 1965. These arrangements were designed to be "watered down" for fans of easy listening music, catering to those who might be offended by the original rock and roll sound. "I mean, really water them down so people who were offended by rock and roll wouldn't be offended by these rock and roll songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Arranger of "The Last Time" String Figure
xref.body: David Whitaker was the orchestrator hired to arrange the string figure in the 1966 Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra's version of The Rolling Stones' "The Last Time." This six-second string figure, which he composed and arranged, became central to The Verve's "Bittersweet Symphony" lawsuit. Despite his pivotal role in creating the sampled material, he received no additional compensation beyond his initial fee in 1966. "They were written and arranged by an orchestrator for higher guy named David Whitaker."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
